newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - The dangers of life after seven pct.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - The dangers of life after seven pct.

text.p: Economies are bouncing and bond markets are in danger of breaking down in the U.S. and Europe, as a seven percent yield on the U.S. long bond beckons, analysts said on Friday.

"We are headed over seven percent," said Michael Burke, senior bond strategist at Citibank International in London. "We have shifted in the United States full focus from solid expansion into outright boom."
U.S. bonds are nervous ahead of key U.S. data later on Friday, after losing nearly a point on Thursday at the long end.
The Dow Jones index also dropped 160.48 points and European bonds and stocks declined after February U.S. retail sales rose a stronger than expected 0.8 percent.
The strong data raised the odds on a tighening in monetary policy at the next Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting on March 25. But analysts said the worry extended beyond that.
"Everyone's talking about a rate rise in March or April," said Tom Hobson, director of technical analysis at Merrill Lynch in London.
"But the back months (in Eurodollar futures) are going down more quickly. That's what drives Treasury markets. It's the fact that they're getting more negative next year."
The 30-year bond was trading at 95-25 at 1005 GMT, to yield 6.96 percent.
February producer prices will be released at 1330 GMT, and are forecast to fall 0.1 percent, according to a Reuters survey, against January's 0.3 percent decline.
"If the producer price data are not weak, yields could push up," said Adam Chester, international bond strategist at Yamaichi International in London.
Chester saw the long bond yield rising to 7.25 percent if U.S. rates rise later this month. The federal funds target rate currently stands at 5.25 percent.
But February industrial production and capacity utilisation data, due at 1415 GMT on Friday, could prove more of a bugbear for bond markets, analysts said, as the data are more forward looking.

Industrial production will have risen 0.5 percent in February, against January's unchanged position, while capacity utilisation will stand at 83.5 percent, compared with January's 83.3 percent, according to a Reuters survey.
"Producers are having to run to catch up with consumers," said Burke.
Data painting a strong picture of the U.S. economy will allow the 10-year T-note/Bund spread to widen from its current 107 basis point level to 120-125 basis points, Chester said.
"At that point, the U.S. market is looking good value."
But other analysts said separate signs of European growth will have a negative impact on bond spreads.
"The newsworthy data will be on the side of European economies picking up in continental Europe," said Alison Cottrell, international economist at PaineWebber International.
German February money supply and producer price data and the IFO industrial survey are expected next week.
"Whatever risk there is with Treasuries will be exacerbated in Europe," added Cottrell, who is based in London.
Other European markets will underperform Germany in a bear trend, analysts said, amid increasing doubts about the timetable for European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
The one exception may be Britain's gilt market, they added, currently trading at a 176 basis point yield spread to Bunds.
Gilts are an attractive prospect as a safe haven from single currency worries, Burke said, and the spread has less room for divergence.
"A 200 basis point spread should keep it in check."
-- Carolyn Cohn, International Bonds Unit +44 171 542 6320
